I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Santiago, Chile at 2026-04-05 06:09 -04 (UTC-0400) (2026-04-05T10:09:00Z in UTC), at latitude -33.4489 degrees and longitude -70.6693 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -10.39 degrees and its azimuth is 89.833 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 48.296 degrees and its azimuth is 271.847 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 89.48 percent illuminated, 142.04 degrees from the Sun, and 398237.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is nautical twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

At 48° above the horizon, the Moon is high in the western sky (azimuth about 272°, essentially due west), so terrain and atmospheric haze near the horizon should not be much of an issue. At nearly 90% illumination it will be a bright waxing/waning gibbous Moon, easily visible to normal unaided eyesight.

Although the Sun is only about 10° below the horizon and the sky is in nautical twilight, a gibbous Moon that high and that far from the Sun (142° elongation) should stand out readily in clear conditions. Look west, roughly halfway between the horizon and straight overhead—slightly closer to overhead than to the horizon.
